authoredSolutions.61:
Apply the three transformations in order.

(a) Reflection of \(P(a,b)\) about \(y=x\) gives \((b,a)\).

(b) Translation of \(2\) units along the positive x-axis gives \((b+2,\,a)\).

(c) Rotation by \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) anticlockwise about the origin, using \((x,y)\mapsto\left(x\cos\frac{\pi}{4}-y\sin\frac{\pi}{4},\;x\sin\frac{\pi}{4}+y\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\) with \(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}=\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\):
\[\left(\frac{(b+2)-a}{\sqrt2},\;\frac{(b+2)+a}{\sqrt2}\right)=\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{7}{\sqrt2}\right).\]

Thus \(b+2-a=-1\Rightarrow b-a=-3\) and \(b+2+a=7\Rightarrow b+a=5\). Solving, \(b=1,\ a=4\).

Therefore \(2a+b=8+1=9\).

Write points on each line: line 1 is \((\alpha+t,\,1+2t,\,1+3t)\) and line 2 is \((4+\beta s,\,6+3s,\,7+3s)\).

Equating the \(y\)- and \(z\)-coordinates at the intersection:
\[1+2t=6+3s\Rightarrow 2t-3s=5,\qquad 1+3t=7+3s\Rightarrow 3t-3s=6.\]
Subtracting gives \(t=s+2\); substituting, \(2(s+2)-3s=5\Rightarrow s=-1,\ t=1\).

The common point must lie on \(x+2y-z=8\). Using line 1's point:
\[(\alpha+t)+2(1+2t)-(1+3t)=8\Rightarrow \alpha+2t+1=8\Rightarrow \alpha=7-2(1)=5.\]
Equating \(x\)-coordinates: \(\alpha+t=4+\beta s\Rightarrow 6=4-\beta\Rightarrow \beta=-2\).

Therefore \(\alpha-\beta=5-(-2)=7\).

The functional equation \(f(x+y)+f(x-y)=2f(x)f(y)\) is the d'Alembert equation, with cosine-type solutions \(f(x)=\cos(cx)\). Setting \(x=y=0\) gives \(2f(0)=2f(0)^2\Rightarrow f(0)=1\).

Using \(f\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=-1\): \(\cos\!\left(\tfrac{c}{2}\right)=-1\Rightarrow c=2\pi\), so \(f(x)=\cos(2\pi x)\). Hence for integer \(k\), \(f(k)=\cos(2\pi k)=1\).

The sum becomes \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{20}\frac{1}{\sin k\,\sin(k+1)}\). Use the identity \(\dfrac{1}{\sin a\,\sin(a+d)}=\dfrac{1}{\sin d}\big(\cot a-\cot(a+d)\big)\) with \(d=1\):
\[\sum_{k=1}^{20}\frac{1}{\sin k\,\sin(k+1)}=\frac{1}{\sin 1}\sum_{k=1}^{20}\big(\cot k-\cot(k+1)\big)=\frac{1}{\sin 1}\big(\cot 1-\cot 21\big).\]

Now \(\cot 1-\cot 21=\dfrac{\cos 1\sin 21-\sin 1\cos 21}{\sin 1\,\sin 21}=\dfrac{\sin 20}{\sin 1\,\sin 21}\). Therefore
\[\text{Sum}=\frac{\sin 20}{\sin^2 1\,\sin 21}=\csc^2(1)\,\csc(21)\,\sin(20).\]

Let \(z=x+iy\). Then \(S_1:(x-2)^2+y^2\le 1\) is the disk of center \((2,0)\), radius \(1\).

For \(S_2\): \(z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)=2(x-y)\), so the condition \(z(1+i)+\bar z(1-i)\ge 4\) becomes \(x-y\ge 2\). The boundary line \(y=x-2\) passes through the center \((2,0)\), so \(S_1\cap S_2\) is the half-disk with \(y\le x-2\).

Maximize \(\left|z-\tfrac52\right|^2=(x-\tfrac52)^2+y^2\) on the circle \(x=2+\cos\theta,\ y=\sin\theta\):
\[f=(\cos\theta-\tfrac12)^2+\sin^2\theta=\tfrac54-\cos\theta.\]
The constraint \(\sin\theta\le\cos\theta\) gives \(\theta\in[-\tfrac{3\pi}{4},\tfrac{\pi}{4}]\). To maximize \(f\), minimize \(\cos\theta\), attained at \(\theta=-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\) where \(\cos\theta=-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\).

Therefore \(f_{\max}=\tfrac54+\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}=\dfrac{5+2\sqrt2}{4}\).

Let \(X\sim\text{Bin}\!\left(8,\tfrac12\right)\), so \(P(X=k)=\dfrac{\binom{8}{k}}{2^8}=\dfrac{\binom{8}{k}}{256}\). The coefficients \(\binom{8}{k}\) for \(k=0,\dots,8\) are \(1,8,28,56,70,56,28,8,1\).

Compute the upper-tail probabilities:
\[P(X\ge 4)=\frac{70+56+28+8+1}{256}=\frac{163}{256}>\frac12,\]
\[P(X\ge 5)=\frac{56+28+8+1}{256}=\frac{93}{256}\approx 0.363<\frac12.\]

So the smallest \(n\) with \(P(X\ge n)<\tfrac12\) is \(n=5\).
